words.def: Something that has both advantages and disadvantages.
ex: Fame is [a double-edged sword]: you get attention, but you lose your privacy.
Working from home can be [a double-edged sword].
Low interest rates are [a double-edged sword] for savers and borrowers.
words.nuance: A double-edged sword stresses that the same feature that helps can also hurt. A mixed blessing is milder: good overall but with drawbacks.
words.ety: A sword sharpened on both edges can cut the person holding it.

prec.s: Social media is ___: it connects people but also spreads hatred faster than ever.
prec.why: A double-edged sword has both good and bad effects. A blessing in disguise is something bad that turns out good; a red herring distracts; a vicious circle is a self-reinforcing problem.

words.def: A question that is no longer relevant because the situation has changed; (UK) an issue open to debate.
words.he: שאלה שאיבדה רלוונטיות; עניין שנוי במחלוקת
ex: Whether we should have hired him is [a moot point] — he's already resigned.
Since the match was cancelled, who would have won is [a moot point].
Whether the policy actually reduced crime remains [a moot point].
words.nuance: In US English, 'moot' mostly means irrelevant now; in UK English, it can also mean still debatable. Note the spelling: moot, not 'mute'.
words.ety: Old English mōt 'meeting' — a 'moot case' was a hypothetical one argued by law students.

prec.s: Whether we should have bought the cheaper tickets is ___ now — the concert has been cancelled.
prec.why: A moot point no longer matters because circumstances changed. A foregone conclusion is a certain outcome; a catch-22 is an impossible situation; the tip of the iceberg is a small visible part of a bigger problem.

words.def: An obvious problem that everyone is aware of but nobody wants to talk about.
ex: The cost of the project is [the elephant in the room].
Nobody mentioned his drinking — it was [the elephant in the room] at every family dinner.
Let's address [the elephant in the room]: we're losing money.
col: address the elephant in the room
ignore the elephant in the room
words.nuance: The elephant in the room is about collective avoidance of an obvious issue. A red herring, by contrast, is a distraction from the real issue.
words.ety: An image of something enormous that everyone pretends not to see; popular since the 1950s.

prec.s: At the meeting everyone discussed new logos, but nobody mentioned ___: the company was nearly bankrupt.
prec.why: The elephant in the room is the obvious problem everyone avoids. The lion's share is the biggest part; a red herring misleads; a moot point is no longer relevant.

words.def: To avoid talking about what is important; to not get to the point.
ex: Stop [beating around the bush] and tell me what happened.
I won't [beat around the bush] — we have to let you go.
He [beat around the bush] for ten minutes before asking for a loan.
words.nuance: British English often says 'beat about the bush'. The opposite is 'cut to the chase' or 'get to the point'.
words.ety: In bird hunting, beaters hit bushes to scare birds out instead of going straight for them.

prec.s: I won't ___: your work this month hasn't been good enough.
prec.why: 'I won't beat around the bush' = I'll say it directly. 'Cut to the chase' means get to the point (so 'I won't cut to the chase' says the opposite); bite the bullet means face something unpleasant; play devil's advocate means argue the other side.

words.def: To force yourself to do something unpleasant or difficult that you have been avoiding.
words.he: לשנס מותניים ולעשות את הלא נעים
ex: I finally [bit the bullet] and booked a dentist appointment.
The company had to [bite the bullet] and cut costs.
Just [bite the bullet] and tell her the truth.
words.nuance: Bite the bullet is accepting something painful but necessary. Face the music is accepting punishment for your own actions; take the plunge is committing to something risky (often positive, like marriage).
words.ety: Possibly from soldiers biting a bullet during surgery without anaesthetic.

prec.s: After years of renting, we decided to ___ and take out a huge mortgage.
prec.why: Bite the bullet = finally do something difficult you've delayed. Face the music means accept punishment; bury the hatchet means make peace; cut corners means do something badly to save time or money. (Take the plunge would also be natural here, which is why it isn't an option.)

words.def: To do something in the easiest, cheapest or fastest way, often ignoring rules or quality.
ex: The builders [cut corners] and the roof started leaking within a year.
Never [cut corners] on safety.
We'll have to [cut corners] to meet the deadline.
words.nuance: Cut corners is always about reducing quality or ignoring proper procedure. A shortcut can be neutral (a quicker route).
words.ety: Like a driver cutting across a corner instead of following the road.

prec.s: The bridge collapsed because the contractor had ___ to save money on steel.
opts: erred on the side of caution
prec.why: Cut corners = reduce quality to save time or money. Go the extra mile means make extra effort; err on the side of caution means be extra careful; bite the bullet means face something unpleasant.

words.word: err on the side of caution
words.ipa: er ɑːn ðə saɪd əv ˈkɔːʃn
words.def: To be extra careful rather than take a risk.
ex: I [erred on the side of caution] and brought an umbrella.
When it comes to children's safety, we [err on the side of caution].
Doctors usually [err on the side of caution] with head injuries.
col: better to err on the side of caution
err on the side of caution and
words.nuance: Err on the side of caution accepts that being too careful is a smaller mistake than being reckless. 'Err' is pronounced like 'air' or 'ur'.
words.ety: err 'make a mistake', from Latin errare 'to wander'.

prec.s: We weren't sure if the ice was thick enough, so we decided to ___ and stay off the lake.
prec.why: Err on the side of caution = choose the safer option. Throw caution to the wind is the opposite; jump on the bandwagon means follow a trend; cut to the chase means get to the point.

words.def: To understand the general meaning of something without all the details.
ex: I didn't understand every word, but I [got the gist].
Can you give me the [gist] of the report?
From her tone, I [got the gist] — she wasn't happy.
words.nuance: The gist is the core meaning. 'Get the drift' is very close and informal; 'the crux' is the most important or difficult point, not the overall meaning.
words.ety: Anglo-French gist 'it lies' — from the legal phrase 'cest action gist' (this action lies), the basis of a case.

prec.s: My Spanish isn't perfect, but I usually ___ of what people are saying.
opts: hit the nail on the head
prec.why: Get the gist = understand the main idea. Hit the nail on the head means say exactly the right thing; beat around the bush means avoid the point; pay lip service to means support in words only.

words.word: hit the nail on the head
words.ipa: hɪt ðə ˈneɪl ɑːn ðə ˈhed
words.def: To describe exactly what is causing a situation or problem; to be exactly right.
words.he: לקלוע בדיוק, לשים את האצבע על הנקודה
ex: You've [hit the nail on the head] — the problem is the price, not the product.
Her review [hit the nail on the head].
I think Sarah [hit the nail on the head] when she said we need more time.
col: you've hit the nail on the head
really hit the nail on the head
words.nuance: Hit the nail on the head praises a precise diagnosis or statement. 'Put your finger on it' is similar but stresses identifying something hard to name.
words.ety: Hitting a nail squarely with a hammer, rather than bending it.

prec.s: 'You've ___,' said the doctor. 'The headaches are caused by your new glasses.'
prec.why: Hit the nail on the head = identify exactly the right cause. Cut corners means do a poor job to save time; jump the gun means act too early; add insult to injury means make a bad situation worse.

words.def: To join an activity or support something because it is popular or fashionable.
ex: Every company is [jumping on the AI bandwagon].
When the team started winning, everyone [jumped on the bandwagon].
Don't just [jump on the bandwagon] — do your own research.
words.nuance: Jump on the bandwagon is usually critical: joining for popularity or profit, not conviction. 'The bandwagon effect' is a term in psychology and economics.
words.ety: In 19th-century US politics, a band played on a wagon in parades; politicians climbed on to share its popularity.

prec.s: As soon as plant-based burgers became popular, every fast-food chain decided to ___.
prec.why: Jump on the bandwagon = join a popular trend. Go the extra mile means make extra effort; bury the hatchet means make peace; play devil's advocate means argue the opposite side.

words.def: Something that seems bad at first but turns out to have good results.
ex: Losing that job was [a blessing in disguise] — I started my own business.
The rain turned out to be [a blessing in disguise]: the crowds stayed home.
Missing the flight was [a blessing in disguise].
col: turn out to be a blessing in disguise
words.nuance: A blessing in disguise is an event that looks bad but is good. A silver lining is a good aspect of an event that stays bad overall.
words.ety: Popularised by an 18th-century hymn by James Hervey.

prec.s: Breaking my leg turned out to be ___: during the recovery I wrote my first novel.
prec.why: A blessing in disguise is a misfortune that turns out well. A double-edged sword has good and bad sides at once; par for the course is normal and expected; a Pyrrhic victory is a win that costs too much.

words.def: To argue against an idea, not because you disagree, but to test it or provoke discussion.
ex: Let me [play devil's advocate] for a moment: what if customers don't want this?
She often [plays devil's advocate] to make the team think harder.
I agree with you, but just to [play devil's advocate]…
words.nuance: Playing devil's advocate signals that the objection is for argument's sake — a polite way to raise a challenge without seeming hostile.
words.ety: The Catholic Church once appointed an official 'devil's advocate' to argue against making someone a saint.

prec.s: I actually like your plan, but let me ___ and list everything that could go wrong.
prec.why: Play devil's advocate = argue against an idea to test it. Sit on the fence means avoid taking sides; beat around the bush means avoid the point; pay lip service means support only in words.

words.def: Something that misleads or distracts from the real issue.
ex: The butler's missing key turned out to be [a red herring].
The debate about the logo is [a red herring]; the real problem is quality.
Detective novels are full of [red herrings].
col: prove to be a red herring
words.nuance: A red herring distracts attention from what matters, deliberately or not. In fiction it's a false clue; in debate it's an irrelevant argument.
words.ety: Strong-smelling smoked (red) herrings were supposedly used to train dogs or throw them off a scent.

prec.s: The argument about immigration was ___; the real cause of the housing crisis was decades of under-building.
prec.why: A red herring distracts from the real issue. The tip of the iceberg is a small visible part of a bigger problem; a foregone conclusion is a certain outcome; a steep learning curve is fast, hard learning.

words.def: A small, visible part of a much larger problem.
ex: The reported cases are just [the tip of the iceberg].
These few complaints may be [the tip of the iceberg].
The fraud they found was only [the tip of the iceberg].
col: just/only the tip of the iceberg
merely the tip of the iceberg
words.nuance: The tip of the iceberg implies that the hidden part is much larger and usually worse.
words.ety: About 90% of an iceberg's mass is below the surface.

prec.s: Police found three fake bank accounts, but they suspect that's only ___.
prec.why: The tip of the iceberg is a small visible part of a much bigger problem. The lion's share is the largest part; the elephant in the room is an ignored obvious issue; 'a far cry from' means very different from.

words.def: A situation in which you cannot succeed because each option depends on the other.
ex: It's [a catch-22]: you need experience to get a job, but you need a job to get experience.
Many refugees face [a catch-22] with documents and work permits.
We're in [a catch-22] situation.
words.nuance: A catch-22 has contradictory rules that block every way out. A dilemma is a hard choice between two options; a vicious circle is a problem that keeps making itself worse.
words.ety: From Joseph Heller's novel 'Catch-22' (1961): a pilot who asks to be excused for insanity proves he is sane.

prec.s: It's ___: the bank won't open an account without an address, and the landlord won't rent without a bank account.
prec.why: A catch-22 is a trap where each requirement depends on the other. A moot point is irrelevant now; a double-edged sword has pros and cons; a blessing in disguise turns out well.

words.def: To avoid becoming close or friendly with someone.
ex: She [keeps her colleagues at arm's length].
The party tried to [keep the controversial donor at arm's length].
After the betrayal, he [kept everyone at arm's length].
words.nuance: Keep at arm's length is deliberate emotional or professional distance. 'An arm's-length transaction' is a business term for a deal between independent parties.
words.ety: Holding someone away at the full length of your arm.

prec.s: Since her divorce, she has ___, refusing every invitation to get close.
prec.why: Keeping people at arm's length means avoiding closeness. Bury the hatchet means make peace; go the extra mile means make extra effort; be on the fence means be undecided.

words.def: Undecided, or unwilling to commit to one side.
ex: I'm still [on the fence] about buying a new car.
Many voters remain [on the fence].
You can't [sit on the fence] forever — choose!
words.nuance: Being on the fence is neutral (undecided). 'Sitting on the fence' is often critical: avoiding a decision to stay safe.
words.ety: Sitting on a fence between two fields, not in either.

prec.s: Two weeks before the election, a third of voters are still ___.
prec.why: On the fence = undecided. In the same boat means sharing a difficult situation; touch and go means uncertain to succeed; by and large means generally.

words.word: cross that bridge when we come to it
words.ipa: krɔːs ðæt ˈbrɪdʒ wen wi kʌm tə ɪt
words.def: To deal with a possible problem only if and when it happens, not worry about it now.
ex: What if it rains? — We'll [cross that bridge when we come to it].
Funding for next year? Let's [cross that bridge when we come to it].
I'd rather [cross that bridge when I come to it].
col: we'll cross that bridge when we come to it
syn: take it one step at a time
words.nuance: Used to calmly postpone worrying about hypothetical problems. The pronoun changes: I'll / we'll / you can cross that bridge…
words.ety: A traveller doesn't need to worry about a bridge still miles ahead.

prec.s: 'What if the buyer pulls out?' — 'Let's not worry yet. We'll ___.'
prec.why: 'Cross that bridge when we come to it' = deal with it only if it happens. Bite the bullet means face something unpleasant now; cut to the chase means get to the point; throw caution to the wind means act recklessly.

words.def: To make a bad situation even worse.
ex: My flight was cancelled, and to [add insult to injury], they lost my luggage.
They fired him, then [added insult to injury] by asking him to train his replacement.
To [add insult to injury], it started to rain.
words.nuance: Add insult to injury usually introduces a second, humiliating misfortune. 'Rub salt in the wound' is about deliberately making someone feel worse.
words.ety: From Aesop's fable of a bald man who, trying to swat a fly on his head, hits himself.

prec.s: We lost 5–0, and to ___, our best player was injured.
opts: hit the nail on the head
prec.why: 'To add insult to injury' introduces something that makes a bad situation worse. The others mean be exactly right, make extra effort, and make peace.

words.def: Very different from something.
ex: Her new flat is [a far cry from] the tiny room she rented as a student.
The final result was [a far cry from] what we'd promised.
Today's smartphones are [a far cry from] the first mobile phones.
words.nuance: A far cry from stresses a large difference, often in quality or standard — improvement or decline.
words.ety: Originally 'a long way', as far as a shout could carry.

prec.s: The five-star resort was ___ the cheap campsites we stayed in as kids.
prec.why: 'A far cry from' means very different from. Par for the course means typical; the tip of the iceberg is a small part of a bigger problem; by and large means generally.

words.def: On the whole; generally, all things considered.
ex: [By and large], the trip was a success.
Students were, [by and large], happy with the course.
[By and large], the reviews have been positive.
words.nuance: By and large allows for exceptions while giving an overall judgement. It's slightly more idiomatic than 'generally'.
words.ety: A sailing term: sailing 'by' (into the wind) and 'large' (with the wind) — handling a ship well in all conditions.

prec.s: There were a few problems with the hotel, but ___, we enjoyed our stay.
prec.why: 'By and large' = overall, generally. To no avail means without success; touch and go means uncertain; on the fence means undecided.

words.def: To get to the most important point without wasting time.
ex: Let's [cut to the chase]: how much will it cost?
I'll [cut to the chase] — we need more money.
He [cut to the chase] and asked her to marry him.
words.nuance: Cut to the chase is a request or decision to skip details. Opposite: beat around the bush.
words.ety: From early Hollywood: editors would 'cut to the chase scene' to skip boring dialogue.

prec.s: We've only got five minutes, so let me ___: we need your signature today.
prec.why: Cut to the chase = go straight to the main point. Beat around the bush is the opposite; pay lip service means support only in words; play devil's advocate means argue the opposite.

words.def: A result that is certain before it happens.
words.he: דבר ידוע מראש, מסקנה ידועה מראש
ex: With the champion injured, the result was [a foregone conclusion].
Her promotion is not [a foregone conclusion].
The election was seen as [a foregone conclusion].
col: by no means a foregone conclusion
words.nuance: Often used in the negative: 'it's by no means a foregone conclusion' = it's not certain. Note the spelling foregone (gone before).
words.ety: From Shakespeare's 'Othello' (1604).

prec.s: With the opposition leader in prison, the election result was ___.
prec.why: A foregone conclusion is a certain result. A moot point is no longer relevant; a red herring is a distraction; a vicious circle is a self-reinforcing problem.

words.def: The largest part of something.
ex: The CEO took [the lion's share] of the profits.
Exports account for [the lion's share] of the company's revenue.
She did [the lion's share] of the work but got none of the credit.
words.nuance: The lion's share often suggests an unfair amount taken by the most powerful. The bulk is neutral.
words.ety: From Aesop's fable in which a lion takes all the prey after hunting with other animals.

prec.s: Although five people worked on the project, the manager took ___ of the bonus.
prec.why: The lion's share is the largest part, often unfairly taken. The tip of the iceberg is a small visible part; 'a far cry' means very different; the elephant in the room is an avoided problem.

words.def: To say you support something without doing anything to help it.
ex: The company [pays lip service to] diversity, but the board is all men.
Politicians [pay lip service to] the environment and then approve new airports.
It's not enough to [pay lip service to] equality.
words.nuance: Pay lip service is about hypocrisy — support in words only. Hebrew has the exact equivalent 'מס שפתיים'.
words.ety: From the Bible (Isaiah 29:13): 'this people honour me with their lips, but have removed their heart far from me'.

prec.s: The government claims to care about mental health, but it only ___ the issue — funding has been cut.
prec.why: Paying lip service to something means supporting it in words only. The others mean argue the other side, get straight to the point, and follow a trend.

words.def: A situation where you have to learn a lot very quickly.
ex: Moving to a new country was [a steep learning curve].
The software has [a steep learning curve], but it's powerful.
Becoming a parent is [a steep learning curve].
words.nuance: In everyday use, 'steep learning curve' means difficult and intense learning. (Technically a steep curve means fast progress, but the everyday meaning has won.)
words.ety: From psychology graphs plotting learning progress against time.

prec.s: My first month as a junior doctor was ___: I had to learn a hundred procedures at once.
prec.why: A steep learning curve = having to learn a lot quickly. Par for the course is normal and expected; a catch-22 is a no-win trap; a blessing in disguise turns out well.

words.word: take with a grain of salt
words.ipa: teɪk wɪð ə ˈɡreɪn əv ˈsɔːlt
words.def: To be sceptical about something; not to believe it completely.
ex: Online reviews should be [taken with a grain of salt].
I [take what he says with a grain of salt] — he exaggerates everything.
The figures should be [taken with a grain of salt].
col: take something with a grain of salt
(UK) take something with a pinch of salt
words.nuance: US English says 'grain of salt'; UK English usually says 'pinch of salt'. Opposite: take at face value.
words.ety: From Latin 'cum grano salis' — Pliny's remedy against poison included a grain of salt.

prec.s: His stories about meeting celebrities are fun, but I'd take them ___.
prec.why: Take something with a grain of salt = don't fully believe it. Take at face value means believe completely; take to heart means be deeply affected; take for granted means fail to appreciate.

words.def: To act in a very risky way, without worrying about the consequences.
ex: We [threw caution to the wind] and spent all our savings on a trip around the world.
For once, she [threw caution to the wind] and said yes.
Investors [threw caution to the wind] during the boom.
col: decide to throw caution to the wind
words.nuance: Throw caution to the wind can be admiring (bold) or critical (reckless). Opposite: err on the side of caution.
words.ety: As if tossing your caution into the wind to be blown away.

prec.s: For once in her careful life, she ___ and bought a one-way ticket to Brazil.
opts: erred on the side of caution
prec.why: Threw caution to the wind = acted boldly without worrying about risks. Err on the side of caution is the opposite; bite the bullet is forcing yourself to do something unpleasant; cut corners is doing a poor job to save effort.

words.def: (Of a situation) very uncertain; risky, with a real chance of a bad result.
ex: It was [touch and go] whether we'd catch the last train.
After the operation, it was [touch and go] for a few days.
The final was [touch and go] until the last minute.
words.nuance: Touch and go is used mostly about outcomes (survival, success, timing) that could easily have gone badly.
words.ety: Possibly from a ship or carriage that touches an obstacle briefly and keeps going.

prec.s: After the accident, it was ___ for a while, but the doctors say he'll make a full recovery.
prec.why: Touch and go = very uncertain, could go either way. By and large means generally; on the fence means undecided; par for the course means normal and expected.

words.def: Without success; with no result.
ex: We searched everywhere for the keys, but [to no avail].
She tried to persuade him, [to no avail].
Doctors tried everything, but [to no avail].
words.nuance: To no avail usually follows an effort described in the sentence. 'In vain' is very close and slightly more literary.
words.ety: avail 'help, benefit', from Old French valoir 'to be worth'.

prec.s: Firefighters battled the blaze all night, but ___; the building was destroyed.
prec.why: 'To no avail' = without success, which matches the destroyed building. By and large means generally; touch and go means uncertain; on the fence means undecided.

words.def: To make more effort than is expected.
ex: Our staff always [go the extra mile] for customers.
She [went the extra mile] and drove me to the airport.
Employers value people who [go the extra mile].
col: go the extra mile for someone
willing to go the extra mile
words.nuance: Go the extra mile is praise for effort beyond duty. Bend over backwards suggests trying extremely hard to please.
words.ety: From the Bible (Matthew 5:41): 'whoever compels you to go one mile, go with him two'.

prec.s: The hotel manager really ___: when my luggage was lost, she lent me clothes and found a pharmacy open at midnight.
prec.why: Went the extra mile = made more effort than expected. Cut corners is doing the minimum badly; jumped on the bandwagon means followed a trend; beat around the bush means avoided the point.

words.def: A situation in which one problem causes another, which then makes the first problem worse.
ex: Poverty and poor health form [a vicious circle].
I can't sleep because I'm stressed, and I'm stressed because I can't sleep — it's [a vicious circle].
Debt can trap families in [a vicious circle].
words.nuance: A vicious circle keeps making itself worse. A catch-22 is a trap of contradictory rules. The opposite is a virtuous circle.
words.ety: From logic: a 'vicious' (faulty) circular argument.

prec.s: Poor sleep makes you anxious, and anxiety ruins your sleep — ___.
prec.why: A vicious circle: each problem makes the other worse. A double-edged sword has both pros and cons; a moot point is irrelevant now; a foregone conclusion is certain.

words.def: Normal or expected, especially of something bad.
ex: Long hours are [par for the course] in this job.
The train was late again — that's [par for the course].
Criticism is [par for the course] for a politician.
words.nuance: Par for the course usually describes something annoying but typical — expressing resignation.
words.ety: From golf: 'par' is the expected number of strokes for a course.

prec.s: Sleepless nights are ___ when you have a newborn baby.
prec.why: Par for the course = typical, to be expected. 'A far cry' means very different; touch and go means uncertain; a red herring is a distraction.

words.def: To end a quarrel and become friendly again.
ex: After years of not speaking, the two brothers finally [buried the hatchet].
It's time to [bury the hatchet] and work together.
The rival companies have [buried the hatchet].
words.nuance: Bury the hatchet is ending a long-running conflict. Make up is for smaller fights, often between friends or couples.
words.ety: From a Native American ceremony of burying weapons to mark peace.

prec.s: After a ten-year feud, the two old bandmates ___ and went on tour together.
opts: kept each other at arm's length
prec.why: Buried the hatchet = ended the quarrel. Keeping someone at arm's length is avoiding closeness; adding insult to injury makes things worse; jumping the gun is acting too early.

words.def: A victory that costs the winner so much that it is hardly worth winning.
ex: Winning the lawsuit was [a Pyrrhic victory] — the legal fees bankrupted the company.
The party won the vote, but it may prove [a Pyrrhic victory].
They took the hill, but it was [a Pyrrhic victory].
words.nuance: A Pyrrhic victory costs more than it gains. A hollow victory feels meaningless, but not necessarily because of its cost.
words.ety: After King Pyrrhus of Epirus, whose victories over Rome in 279 BC destroyed most of his army.

prec.s: He won custody of the house, but after three years of legal fees it was ___.
prec.why: A Pyrrhic victory is a win that costs so much it's hardly worth it. A blessing in disguise is a misfortune that turns out well; par for the course is typical; a steep learning curve is intense learning.
